A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MELD research work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite substantial revision and reorganization.

before.justification: v3 reports original molecular-generation results, scheduling ablations, and qualitative and diffusion-step analyses in Tables 1–3 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v4 reports revised molecular-generation results and additional original Guacamol, SBM, state-clashing, embedding, and computational-cost experiments.

M1.justification: Section 3.3 replaces v3's weighted polynomial-basis schedule and sigmoid transformation with a power-law schedule using a learned softplus-transformed exponent and epsilon floor. This changes the central corruption-scheduling component. The embedding-based approach, joint optimization, denoising framework, and straight-through Gumbel-Softmax training remain.

E1.justification: v4 retains QM9, ZINC250K, and property-conditioned Polymer generation, while adding Guacamol molecular generation and SBM synthetic-graph generation. These extend evaluation to larger-scale molecular data and a non-molecular domain with different node and edge semantics.

E2.justification: Tables 1–2 add a fixed power-law MDM baseline. Table 3 replaces its fixed polynomial reference with power-law and adds DiffusionBERT and TabDiff; GenMD4 corresponds to v3's existing class-wise ablation. The new Guacamol comparison also includes ConGress and DisCo. These substantially broaden the evaluated alternatives.

E3.justification: Figure 4 changes its diagnostic from coefficient of variation to standard deviation, and Table 3 replaces separate validity, uniqueness, and novelty columns with V.U.N. New protocols include Guacamol's transformed metrics and 300-versus-1000-epoch MELD/DiGress comparison, SBM graph-statistic MMD, sampled graph-isomorphism checks, and cost profiling across 10–200 atoms. The original 10K-sample molecular evaluations remain.

E4.justification: v4 adds node-only and edge-only scheduling ablations, direct state-clashing counts on ZINC250K and SBM, learned-versus-random-walk embedding analysis, and computational scaling analysis. Entropy and reconstruction examples are revised. The diffusion-step robustness study already existed in v3 Appendix D.1 and is retained, with updated plots, in v4 Appendix D.3.

E5.justification: Both versions retain the implementation statement specifying seed 0. v4 additionally reports three-seed averages for state-clashing counts in Tables 5 and 9, and five-seed runtime averages with plus/minus values in Table 10. Comparable uncertainty reporting is not added to the main generation tables.

E6.justification: Many results are replaced. MELD's QM9 FCD changes from 0.64 to 0.09; ZINC250K validity/FCD changes from 93.21/2.24 to 100.00/1.51, while NSPDK changes from 0.0006 to 0.0008. Polymer MAE changes from 0.769 to 0.798 and FCD from 6.17 to 5.93. Fixed cosine/polynomial ZINC250K validity changes from 14.58/27.78 to 100/100. Additional benchmarks and analyses supply new outcomes. These revisions do not establish gains from a single controlled change.

T1.justification: The mathematical schedule definition is replaced in Section 3.3. Equation 3 and the posterior factorization also change edge indexing from all i,j pairs to i<j, excluding diagonal and duplicate pairs in the stated formulation. The KL-based state-clashing argument and straight-through derivation remain; no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract shifts from rescuing ZINC250K validity from approximately 15% to 93% to claiming the first diffusion-based generator with 100% validity on QM9 and ZINC250K. The introduction adds large-scale molecular and synthetic-graph generalization claims, while the claimed Polymer alignment advantage narrows from 16.5% to 13.4%. The previous contribution about node-first reconstruction and late scheduling variation is removed.

C2.justification: v4 emphasizes distributional mismatch despite valid outputs, replacing much of v3's invalid-molecule interpretation. It drops the node-first reconstruction and late variation-peak interpretations, adds a tractability rationale against conditioning schedules on corrupted graphs, and discusses smaller expected benefits in other discrete domains. Appendix B retains the existing residual-clashing limitation but newly asserts that these remaining clashes do not compromise overall efficacy.

D1.justification: v4 newly documents training-time permutation of embedding columns, the power-law stability constant, Guacamol's training budget, and profiling hardware. Most backbone and optimizer details remain unchanged. Conversely, v3's explicit node/edge scheduler projections, optional property concatenation, and hydrogen-exclusion statement are no longer documented; their omission does not establish corresponding implementation changes.

R1.justification: v4 adds references including DiffusionBERT, TabDiff, Guacamol, SPECTRE, DisCo, and graph-isomorphism work, while removing some background references such as Campbell et al. and DiffuSeq. Appendix A adds feature-wise scheduling and sharpens the contrast with Schrödinger bridges. The central positioning around element-wise scheduling and state-clashing remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contribution list, and results narrative are extensively rewritten. Baseline and metric descriptions move from Section 4.1 to Appendix C, and the scheduling-variation discussion moves from Section 4.4 to Appendix D.2. The experimental narrative and appendix organization are substantially reworked, beyond simply inserting new results.

P2.justification: Table 3 is redesigned with named scheduling methods and new columns, and six substantive tables are added; v3's dataset-statistics table survives as Table 7. Figures 2–7 are revised, including new examples, trajectory panels, Figure 4's changed axis and relocation, and zero-based axes in Figure 5. Figure 7 receives a separate page, and the document adopts different typography and Preprint headers.

improvement.justification: Direct state-clashing measurements and broader scheduling controls strengthen evidence for the central mechanism beyond v3's largely illustrative analyses; Guacamol and SBM also test previously unexamined scope. These are useful net gains, tempered by reporting weaknesses: fixed-baseline validity changes are unexplained, Table 1 gives those controls the same headline 100% validity, and the new negligible-overhead characterization overlooks Table 10's 25% runtime increase at 200 atoms.
